authors: Verbeek H, Gerritsen DL, Backhaus R, de Boer BS, Koopmans RTCM, Hamers JPH
title: Allowing Visitors Back in the Nursing Home During the COVID-19 Crisis: A Dutch National Study Into First Experiences and Impact on Well-Being
venue: Journal of the American Medical Directors Association 21(7):900-904
setting: 26 Dutch nursing homes piloting the reopening to visitors after the COVID-19 visitor ban (first 2 weeks of the pilot; infection follow-up covered May 11-June 5 2020); contact persons were managers, quality/policy officers and registered nurses
speaker: Team leader, Nursing Home 26
quote: Mister J. did not recognize his son as they had not seen each other for 10 weeks… He was crying and could not understand how he could forget about his son.
nametags_relevance: Supports the core announcement use case and open tension 4 (long separations), and shows the harm was the resident's distress at having forgotten his son, so how an announcement like "That's David, your grandson" is worded matters as much as getting the name right.
note: Read in the full text, Results, in a disp-quote block that follows the authors' sentence 'In some cases, it was reported that residents did not recognize their family due to the long period of visit restrictions.' The source has a non-breaking space in '10 weeks' and a single ellipsis character; both are kept. The sentences after the quote ('For the son, this was difficult too.') are not quoted. Europe PMC flags it open access (Elsevier COVID-19 collection), with no CC licence listed.

authors: Bernardi S, Fiordelli M, Rubinelli S, Spagnoli V, Malacrida R, Martignoni G
title: Navigating Communication in Nursing Homes During COVID-19: Perspectives From Families, Healthcare Professionals, and Managers in Southern Switzerland-A Qualitative Study
setting: Nursing homes in Canton Ticino and Moesano (Italian-speaking southern Switzerland); interviews June-August 2020 with family members, healthcare professionals and managers about the March-June 2020 closures
speaker: Nurse, male, more 10
quote: You see, there are small gestures. Maybe [the family member] tends to lower the mask to make themselves recognizable because even there, seeing the eyes is fine, but facial expressions are not the same
nametags_relevance: Open tension 4 (masks): residents needed the visitor's face to recognize them, which is the case where Nametags' voice-first presence (a voice counts at once; the camera names a face after two sightings and breaks ties between close voices) matters most and where face matching should be tested on masked faces.
note: Table 4, row B9, read in the raw XML table: columns are quote ID, quote, source; the source column is 'Nurse, male, more 10' (role, gender, years of experience as the table footnote explains). The source quote has no final full stop; none was added. The square-bracket insertion is in the source. The authors' summary sentence says these visits 'impeded nonverbal communication, especially for residents with cognitive decline (who found it challenging to recognize family members)'. Row B10 (a family member who was not recognized in a cap, mask, gloves and gown) and row F9 (a resident who 'practically didn't recognize any of her children anymore') are attributed to family members in the table, so they are not used here.

authors: Kaelen S, van den Boogaard W, Pellecchia U, Spiers S, De Cramer C, Demaegd G, Fouqueray E, Van den Bergh R, Goublomme S, Decroo T, Quinet M, Van Hoof E, Draguez B
title: How to bring residents' psychosocial well-being to the heart of the fight against Covid-19 in Belgian nursing homes-A qualitative study
setting: Eight nursing homes in Brussels; focus groups with direct care staff plus 56 resident interviews, June 2020
speaker: authors' summary
quote: The masks created even more distance, as many residents did not recognize the staff anymore or could no longer engage in a conversation due to hearing problems.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 4 (masks): the people residents stopped recognizing were staff, who are not part of the family-led enrollment that product.md describes.
note: Authors' summary of the staff focus groups (Results, 'Re-organization of work'); no direct staff quote on recognition. Caveat: the passage does not say these residents had dementia, and the resident interviews excluded anyone scoring under 24 on the MMSE (the authors' limitations say the experiences of people with dementia were not included). Use it for masks and staff recognition, not as evidence about dementia specifically.

authors: Ariander A, Olaison A, Andersson C, Sjödahl R, Nilsson L, Kastbom L
title: Ethical challenges causing moral distress: nursing home staff's experiences of working during the COVID-19 pandemic
venue: Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care 42(2):266-275
setting: Ten long-term nursing homes, including dementia care homes, in Östergötland; 20 staff interviews (physicians, nurses, nurse assistants) in February-April 2022 about working during the pandemic
speaker: authors' summary
quote: Wearing the protective equipment could also make staff feel that residents did not recognize them, particularly when caring for residents with cognitive impairments.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 4 (masks/PPE): staff felt that residents, particularly those with cognitive impairment, did not recognize them in protective equipment, a case for naming staff by voice, but staff are not in the family-led enrollment that product.md describes.
note: Authors' summary in Results ('Balancing restrictions and allocation of scarce resources with care needs'); the paper gives no direct staff quote on recognition. Interviews were held in 2022, looking back on the pandemic.

authors: Kemp CL, Anglin E, Morgan JC, Perkins MM, Burgess EO, Bender AA
title: Differing Realities Among Assisted Living Residents With Dementia: Understanding Care Partner Responses
setting: Eight assisted living communities in and around Atlanta, Georgia; 73 residents with dementia and 103 care partners; each community studied for 1 year between 2019 and 2023, with an 18-month pause from March 2020
speaker: authors' summary
quote: In all communities, we observed residents believing that certain staff members were “relatives” and “good friends” or had long-standing family connections. Care partners tended not to correct these misconceptions viewing them signs of “trust” that made residents “receptive to care.”
nametags_relevance: Open tension 1: in all eight communities residents believed some staff were relatives, and care partners tended not to correct this because it made residents receptive to care, so a truthful announcement of a staff member's name and role would contradict a belief they deliberately left alone.
note: Authors' observational summary (Results, 'Joining'). The same paragraph says 'Certain family members and most staff, however, played along with resident-assigned roles.' The paper is not one-sided: under 'Correcting' it reports truth telling that helped some residents (a care worker reminding a resident her husband had died) and harmed others. covid_period is set false because the study is not about COVID-19 and fieldwork began in 2019, before the March 2020 pause, so 'all communities' includes pre-pandemic fieldwork (an inference from the stated dates); part of the fieldwork did fall in 2021-2023. Free to read in PMC but not open-access licensed; the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint returned HTTP 500 and NCBI efetch withholds the body, so text_url is the PMC article page. The publisher page and Europe PMC's article page both return HTTP 403 to scripts.

authors: Kemp CL, Anglin E, Morgan JC, Perkins MM, Burgess EO, Bender AA
title: Differing Realities Among Assisted Living Residents With Dementia: Understanding Care Partner Responses
setting: Oakwood Forest (pseudonym), one of eight assisted living communities in and around Atlanta, Georgia; study fieldwork 2019-2023 with an 18-month pause from March 2020
speaker: care worker
quote: If you want to communicate with Hugh, you are his assistant. He would tell you he has a meeting; you just tell him that you’ll schedule that for him.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 1: this care worker gets Hugh to accept care by taking the role he assigns her (his assistant), which an arrival announcement of her real name and role could disrupt.
note: Blockquote introduced by 'At Oakwood Forest, a care worker described Hugh, a retired executive, and the significance of engaging in his reality'. Hugh is the paper's pseudonym. The rest of the quote, not used, ends with the worker asking him to take his medication (the source spells it 'mediation'). Same access situation as the other Kemp entry: text_url is the PMC article page because Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 500.

authors: Cohen-Mansfield J, Golander H, Arnheim G, Cohen R
title: Reactions and Interventions for Delusions in Nursing Home Residents with Dementia
venue: American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias 29(4):386-394
setting: Eight nursing homes; paid staff informants (registered and practical nurses, nurse aides, occupational workers, administrators) reported on 38 residents with dementia who had delusions, June 2007-January 2009
speaker: authors' summary
quote: For example, Mr D, an 81-year-old man with an MMSE score of 17, experiences a misidentification delusion in which he thinks one of the caregivers is his daughter and at times mistook his son for his older brother. The informant concluded that no intervention was needed as the delusion neither had negative consequences nor was it accompanied by any emotional discomfort.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 1: the staff informant concluded that no intervention was needed when a resident took a caregiver for his daughter and his son for his brother, whereas Nametags would name the son and his relationship when he arrives.
note: Results, 'Agree' section; it is the authors' account of what one staff informant reported. Mr D and the age/MMSE details are printed in the source. Table 1, read in the full text, backs the '60%' figure in product.md: for misidentification delusions (n = 5) staff agreed 60%, argued 40%, calmed 40% and explained 0%. The text confirms explaining 'was not used with any of the participants with delusions of abandonment, misidentification, and other delusions.' With n = 5, 60% means 3 cases. Free to read in PMC but not open-access licensed; Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 500 and efetch withholds the body, so text_url is the PMC article page. The SAGE page and Europe PMC's article page return HTTP 403 to scripts.

authors: Cohen-Mansfield J, Golander H, Arnheim G, Cohen R
title: Reactions and Interventions for Delusions in Nursing Home Residents with Dementia
venue: American Journal of Alzheimer's Disease and Other Dementias 29(4):386-394
setting: Eight nursing homes; paid staff informants reported on 38 residents with dementia who had delusions, June 2007-January 2009
speaker: authors' summary
quote: The converse reaction is arguing with the older person about reality by telling the person that he or she is wrong, which occurred in 37% of the cases. This was the reaction in half the cases of delusion of theft and for 40% of the instances when a person manifested delusions of misidentification and when thinking the house was not their home.
nametags_relevance: Qualifies open tension 1: staff did tell residents they were wrong in 40% of misidentification cases, so 'staff go along 60% of the time' should be cited with its base of 5 cases and with the 40% who corrected.
note: Results, 'Argue' section. Added as a counterweight to the 60% agreeing figure product.md cites from the same table; both percentages share the same 5 misidentification delusions, and a delusion could get more than one reaction. Same access situation and text_url as the other Cohen-Mansfield entry.

title: The experience of lying in dementia care: a qualitative study
setting: Five residential aged care facilities in Queensland; registered and enrolled nurses, personal care assistants and allied health professionals (data-collection dates are not in the abstract)
speaker: authors' summary
quote: Care providers in residential aged care facilities (RACFs) lie to residents with dementia. Lying is conceptualized as therapeutic whereby the care provider's intent is to eliminate harm and also control behaviour.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 2: staff treat lying as a therapeutic tool, while Nova may 'Never guess or invent a fact', and the paper's own proposal promotes truth telling first while keeping the lie as an option.
note: Abstract only: the article is not in PMC and is subscription-only, so the full text was not read. The abstract was read in the Europe PMC core record at text_url (abstractText field). The abstract's last sentence proposes 'A complimentary four stage communication strategy that promotes truth telling as a first option while also recommending the lie as a suitable strategy'. Published online 2011-12-02; issue year 2012.

authors: Edwards KJ, Jones RB, Shenton D, Page T, Maramba I, Warren A, Fraser F, Križaj T, Coombe T, Cowls H, Chatterjee A
title: The Use of Smart Speakers in Care Home Residents: Implementation Study
setting: Care homes in Cornwall, South West England, offered free smart speakers (Amazon Echo Spot / Kindle Fire); feedback by staff diaries and a telephone survey, mostly from managers; device chosen in December 2018, support contacts April 2019-February 2020, phone survey early 2020
speaker: authors' summary
quote: Nine (8%) homes reported device limitations including the smart speaker’s inability to understand certain residents because of speech difficulties or not using the “desired” language.
nametags_relevance: Nova depends on a wake word and speech transcription from the wearer, and nine care homes reported that a commercial voice assistant could not understand some residents with speech difficulties, so Nova should be tested with impaired speech.
note: Results, read in the full text. Not dementia-specific: the homes were mostly care homes for older people, plus homes for physical or mental health needs, and dementia is mentioned once, in the Discussion. In the same section, 4 homes reported temporary confusion or dislike, and one respondent said residents were 'a little suspicious of the speaker' at first but came to 'take it in their stride'. The authors say feedback came 'primarily from one person, usually the manager'.

authors: Edwards KJ, Jones RB, Shenton D, Page T, Maramba I, Warren A, Fraser F, Križaj T, Coombe T, Cowls H, Chatterjee A
title: The Use of Smart Speakers in Care Home Residents: Implementation Study
setting: Care homes in Cornwall, South West England, offered free smart speakers; telephone survey early 2020
speaker: authors' summary
quote: Among the 35 care homes that reported not using the device, 15 (43%) belonged to a care provider whose IT specialist raised concerns about data protection (Multimedia Appendix 2).
nametags_relevance: Tension 5 and 'what leaves the device': data-protection objections from one provider's IT kept the device unused in 15 of the 35 non-using homes, and Nova sends questions to Anthropic and transcripts to Gemini, so the data path will need documenting for care-home IT.
note: Results ('barriers'), read in the full text. The paper does not say whose data the IT specialist was concerned about; the 'bystander privacy' tag is my mapping to the closest theme. The Discussion adds that 'smart speaker use in communal areas of care homes for mainly entertainment purposes creates few privacy concerns'. Not dementia-specific.

authors: Koh WQ, Vandemeulebroucke T, Gastmans C, Miranda R, Van den Block L
title: The ethics of pet robots in dementia care settings: Care professionals' and organisational leaders' ethical intuitions
setting: Eight nursing homes; interviews with 12 care professionals and 10 organisational leaders about pet robots in routine dementia care, August-November 2021 (secondary analysis)
speaker: care professional [CP10]
quote: you don’t actually want somebody… associating with it as if it was a real animal because that could cause further distress down the line if they feel, well, I’ve never seen it eating or it doesn’t seem to be drinking… they could be stressors to the person with dementia… I think in so far as is possible you’d want to be introducing it that it is a robot
nametags_relevance: Open tension 2: this care professional wanted the robot introduced as a robot to prevent later distress, which argues against Nova's 'Never mention being an AI unless asked'.
note: Findings, individual-relational level, under Theme 2 ('Care providers’ autonomy and wellbeing'). The authors introduce it as 'One care professional expressed that residents’ misperception of pet robots as real animals may lead them to experience distress'. It is a minority view: the authors' summary table says 'Few were concerned that residents’ misperceptions of them as real animals may lead residents to experience distress'. The leading ellipsis and the closing ' [CP10].' are left out; the interior ellipses are the source's. The table of roles does not map CP numbers to roles (care professionals were nurses, a healthcare assistant, activity coordinators, occupational therapists and a physiotherapist). Interviews took place during the pandemic, but the topic is not COVID-19.

authors: Koh WQ, Vandemeulebroucke T, Gastmans C, Miranda R, Van den Block L
title: The ethics of pet robots in dementia care settings: Care professionals' and organisational leaders' ethical intuitions
setting: Eight nursing homes; interviews with care professionals and organisational leaders, August-November 2021
speaker: care professional [CP5]
quote: we will say it to our residents “is little kitten okay here in the basket or is he okay here.” if that’s their reality and they believe the cat is real. they’re happy with that
nametags_relevance: Open tension 2, the other side: staff who used the robots spoke of the robot cat as real when residents believed it was, and most participants supported going along with that, so Nova not volunteering that it is an AI matches what many staff already do with robots.
note: Findings, Theme 3 ('Social facilitation and connecting with residents'), introduced by the authors' sentence 'When conversing with residents about the pet robots, participants appeared to go along with their reality, speaking about the robots as if they were real animals'. The authors' summary table says 'Most were in support of “going with residents” reality of treating pet robots as real animals'. The quote is transcribed with lowercase sentence starts, kept exactly; the leading ellipsis and closing ' [CP5].' are left out.

authors: Emilsson M, Karlsson C, Svensson A
title: Experiences of using surveillance cameras as a monitoring solution at nursing homes: The eldercare personnel's perspectives
setting: Three nursing homes in a small, sparsely populated municipality, most residents with cognitive impairment; 44 of about 50 residents had night-time room cameras; 16 staff interviewed (all assistant nurses except the unit manager) at the end of 2019
speaker: assistant nurse, night shift (IP 3)
quote: Some felt uncomfortable that we should maybe be on film, did someone sit and watch us? We joked about it, that we must look good in the hair before going to work.
nametags_relevance: Open tension 3: night staff were uneasy at merely possibly being filmed by fixed room cameras, while Nametags' glasses film and transcribe staff in every encounter, so staff consent has to be part of any care-home deployment.
note: Results, 'Prerequisites for implementation'. The authors summarize: 'Some members of the staff felt uncomfortable being on film, and with the idea that someone could sit and watch them'; staff later learned the cameras were not recording all the time. Interviews were 'at the end of 2019, just before the pandemic began'. IP 3's role comes from Table 1 (night shift) and the text ('All participants except the unit manager were assistant nurses'). Also under 'Importance of integrity', a night-shift assistant nurse (IP 9) says 'I know someone who has hung a cap over it [the camera], for example, because they feel monitored'; it is not clear whether that person was a resident or a relative.

authors: Rönning H, Svanholm S, Ekdahl A, Johansson D, Rising MH
title: "To Have One Extra Eye": Exploring Professionals' Experiences with Digital Supervision in a Nursing Home for Older People
setting: One municipal nursing home (32 apartments; residents include people with dementia) in a small municipality in east-central Sweden, using wall-mounted sensor-based digital supervision; 28 professionals interviewed February-November 2024
speaker: authors' summary
quote: The device, which was mounted on the wall of the resident's apartment, might have gone unnoticed by the residents as time passed. Although the professionals had informed the residents about the system, they acknowledged that residents were likely to forget about it, “…it's not just once, but it can be every time you come in as it can change for someone with cognitive impairment” (Nr 10).
nametags_relevance: Open tension 3: residents who had been told about in-room monitoring were likely to forget it, so a one-time notice to residents and visitors that the wearer's glasses carry a camera and microphone will not stay known.
note: Results, last paragraph. The authors' summary embeds a professional's words (interview Nr 10, role not given), so quote_is_staff is false. The system's sensors generated a room layout, and professionals 'could not view body details but could observe movement patterns', which they saw as preserving residents' anonymity; images were saved only on fall alarms. Published 2026 (online 2026-03-24); found and read via Europe PMC.

authors: Murray J, Thompson J, Hill M, James I
title: An ethnographic study to develop a taxonomy of lies for communicating with people with moderate to severe dementia
setting: Two hospital wards for people with moderate to severe dementia in North East England; 338 hours of participant observation over 4 months; 250 lies recorded from 63 professional caregivers
speaker: authors' summary
quote: As soon as the healthcare assistant was out of sight, the patient stopped shouting. There was no recognition when they came back into the room.
nametags_relevance: Relevant to Nova's truthfulness rules and to the re-announce window (the patient did not recognize the healthcare assistant who had just left), but it does not meet the care-home setting criterion.
note: Dropped because the setting is hospital wards, not a care home, nursing home or assisted living. Otherwise strong on going along: six categories of lie ('blatant, avoidance, familiarity, props, banter and going along with'). The quote is from a field-note example of a spontaneous 'going along with' lie. The paper does not state the data-collection dates, so covid_period=false is not verified.

authors: Eikelenboom-Boskamp A, Huis A, Saris K, Stobernack T, de Leeuw M, Hulscher M, Voss A
title: Preferences for healthcare worker attire among nursing home residents and residents' preferences as perceived by workers: A cross-sectional study
venue: International Journal of Nursing Studies Advances 5:100112
setting: 10 Dutch nursing homes; 94 participants (residents with physical impairments and no known dementia, and their nurses), February-October 2019
speaker: authors' summary
quote: However, we know that the wording on name badges is small and unreadable by most residents, so we do not know whether this would have influenced the preferences. Furthermore, name badges are often not worn due to risks attached with moving and handling patients.
nametags_relevance: If name badges really are unreadable to most residents and often not worn, a spoken name is a plausible substitute, but this is an unsupported aside, not evidence.
note: Dropped because it is the authors' unreferenced aside in the Limitations, not a staff account, and the study deliberately excluded residents with a known dementia diagnosis. It was the only name-badge passage in the papers read for step 2.
